p: Hussite Prague: the Four Articles of Prague (communion in both kinds, free preaching) are proclaimed after the 1419 defenestration
After the Battle of White Mountain the Habsburgs re-Catholicise Bohemia; Protestant worship banned (Renewed Land Ordinance 1627)
Radical Hussites (Taborites) found the town of Tábor
George of Poděbrady takes Tábor; the radical Taborite community ends
Compacts of Basel: the Church accepts Utraquist (Hussite) communion in Bohemia and Moravia (centroid of Bohemia)
Renewed Land Ordinance makes Catholicism the only permitted faith; Protestant nobles must convert or emigrate
The Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum), heirs of the Hussites, is founded here
After White Mountain the Brethren are banned and expelled; Comenius leads many into exile
Wittenberg's council issues the first evangelical church ordinance after Karlstadt's Christmas 1521 communion in both kinds
Elector John the Steadfast orders church visitations that organise a Lutheran territorial church (capital Torgau)
Duke Henry the Pious introduces the Reformation in Albertine Saxony after his Catholic brother George dies (capital Dresden)
Luther preaches at Pentecost 1539 as Albertine Saxony turns Protestant
Georg Petz becomes the first evangelical pastor; most of the city turns Protestant, though it stays under the Catholic Archbishop of Mainz
Halle's council calls Justus Jonas and adopts the Reformation against Cardinal Albrecht
Magdeburg's citizens adopt the Reformation after Luther preaches there
Prince Wolfgang of Anhalt-Köthen, an early Luther supporter, introduces the Reformation (capital Köthen)
Landgrave Philip of Hesse holds the Synod of Homberg and founds Marburg, the first Protestant university, in 1527
Landgrave Maurice moves Hesse-Kassel from Lutheran to Reformed (Calvinist) worship
Elector Joachim II takes communion in both kinds and introduces a Lutheran church order; his heir Johann Sigismund turns Reformed in 1613
Albert of Prussia secularises the Teutonic Order's state into the first Lutheran duchy (capital Königsberg)
Margrave George the Pious introduces the Reformation (capital Ansbach)
Duke Ernest the Confessor introduces the Reformation; he signs the Augsburg Confession in 1530 (capital Celle)
Duke Julius introduces the Reformation after the death of his Catholic father Henry the Younger (capital Wolfenbüttel)
Duke Ulrich, restored by Philip of Hesse, introduces the Reformation (capital Stuttgart)
Bugenhagen's church order is adopted in 1534/35 (capital Stettin)
The Diet at Sternberg confirms Lutheranism as the faith of the duchy (capital Schwerin)
Elector Frederick III issues the Heidelberg Catechism, making the Palatinate Reformed (Lutheran since 1556; capital Heidelberg)
The Reformation is introduced with the Palatine church order under Elector Otto Henry (capital Amberg)
Bavaria occupies it (1621), re-Catholicises it and annexes it (1628); Protestants who will not convert must leave
Count John VI makes Nassau-Dillenburg Reformed and founds the Calvinist Herborn Academy (1584)
After a religious colloquy in March 1525 the city council adopts the Reformation
Under Martin Bucer's influence the council abolishes the Mass in February 1529
The council introduces the Reformation in 1534/37; after the Interim (1548) and the 1555 peace Augsburg becomes a biconfessional city
Heinrich von Zütphen preaches the first Reformation sermon (November 1522); the city turns Lutheran and later Reformed
Bugenhagen's church order is adopted by the city
Bugenhagen's church order is adopted in the leading Hanseatic city
The city adopts Bugenhagen's church order
The council introduces the Reformation and calls Nikolaus von Amsdorf; first church order 1531
In a citizens' vote (November 1530) 1,621 of 1,865 voters choose the Reformation; Ambrosius Blarer introduces it in 1531
The free imperial city introduces the Reformation
The imperial city's council introduces the Reformation
The Twelve Articles of the peasants are drafted here; the city turns Protestant in the 1520s
Matthäus Alber, preaching Luther's teaching from 1519, makes Reutlingen a Protestant stronghold; it joins the 1529 Protestation
Johannes Brenz reforms the city's church
Ambrosius Blarer and Johannes Zwick reform the city; the bishop leaves
Habsburg troops take Constance after it refuses the Interim; it is re-Catholicised and loses its imperial freedom
Johann Hess is appointed pastor and Breslau (Wrocław) adopts the Reformation
John a Lasco leads the East Frisian church; Emden becomes a refuge for Dutch Calvinists ('Geneva of the North')
Archbishop-Elector Hermann von Wied invites Bucer and Melanchthon to reform his territory (residence Bonn)
Wied is deposed and excommunicated; the electorate stays Catholic
At the Grünwald conference (February 1522) the dukes decide Bavaria stays Catholic; Luther's followers are arrested or expelled (capital Munich)
Prince-Bishop Julius Echter banishes Lutheran preachers and leads the Counter-Reformation (Jesuit-run university 1582)
The Pacification of Graz grants the Styrian Protestant nobility freedom of worship
Archduke Ferdinand orders Protestant pastors and teachers expelled and sends commissions to restore Catholic parishes
Maximilian II offers the Austrian estates a religious concession (1568; assurance 1571) allowing Lutheran worship for nobles and their subjects
After the Bohemian Revolt is crushed, Austria's Protestant nobles and clergy are expelled or forced to convert
By 1550 most people in Upper Austria are Protestant (capital Linz)
Under Bavarian occupation an imperial reformation commission expels Protestant preachers; resentment fuels the Peasants' War of 1626
Primož Trubar, expelled from Ljubljana in 1547, writes the first two books in Slovene (1550); Carniola's estates turn largely Protestant
Bishop Thomas Chrön suppresses Protestantism in his diocese (1600–1603)
Archbishop Wolf Dietrich expels all Protestants from the city
Pope Paul III founds the Roman Inquisition to stop the spread of Protestant ideas in Italy
City council adopts Zwingli's reform after the First Disputation (January 1523)
Swiss Brethren perform the first adult baptisms (January 1525) and form the first Anabaptist congregation
Zürich drowns Felix Manz, the first Anabaptist executed by Protestants
Swiss Brethren agree the Schleitheim Confession, the first Anabaptist statement of faith
Balthasar Hubmaier leads the town into Anabaptism
Austrian troops retake Waldshut in December 1525; Hubmaier flees
The Bern Disputation leads the largest Swiss city-state to adopt the Reformation
After iconoclastic riots the council adopts the Reformation under Oecolampadius
Joachim Vadian, elected mayor in 1526, leads the city into the Reformation
William Farel's preaching leads the town to vote for the Reformation
The citizens vote in May 1536 to 'live according to the Gospel'; Calvin arrives that summer
Bern conquers Vaud and imposes the Reformation; the cathedral is stripped
The Ilanz Articles let each commune of the Three Leagues choose its faith; many turn Reformed
The Catholic inner cantons defeat Zürich at Kappel; Zwingli is killed, the Swiss stay split by confession
A small Protestant community forms in the Italian-speaking town
The Catholic cantons expel the Protestants; about 100 exiles move to Zürich
Protestant communities grow under rule of the Grisons, many founded by Italian religious refugees
Catholic rebels kill 300–600 Protestants in the 'Sacro Macello' (18–23 July 1620)
Duke Christian (later Christian III) issues the Haderslev Ordinance, the first Lutheran church order in the Danish lands
Gustav Vasa's Riksdag of Västerås breaks the Church's power and allows Lutheran preaching
Olaus Petri preaches in Stockholm; the Swedish New Testament is printed
The Uppsala Synod adopts the Augsburg Confession, making Sweden firmly Lutheran
As part of Sweden, Finland follows the Västerås decisions; Mikael Agricola prints the Finnish New Testament in 1548 (capital Turku)
Christian III arrests the bishops and makes Denmark Lutheran; the church ordinance follows in 1537
Archbishop Olav Engelbrektsson flees and the Danish Lutheran church order is imposed on Norway
The southern Icelandic diocese accepts the Lutheran church order
Bishop Jón Arason, last Catholic bishop of Iceland, is beheaded; the north turns Lutheran
Riga accepts the Reformation, ending the archbishops' power
Livonian towns and knights meeting in Reval (July 1524) resolve to keep the Protestant teaching; iconoclasm follows in September
Gotthard Kettler secularises the Livonian Order's lands into the Lutheran Duchy of Courland (capital Mitau)
Lutheran preaching from 1522 (a 1525 uprising is crushed); in 1557 King Sigismund II Augustus confirms communion in both kinds
Royal Prussian Toruń receives the right to Lutheran worship
The first Calvinist service in Poland-Lithuania is held here (1550) after the town's lord expels the monks
Founded as the centre of the anti-Trinitarian Polish Brethren; the Racovian Catechism is printed in 1605
The Sejm closes the Raków Academy and press; Polish Brethren are expelled in 1658
Mikołaj Radziwiłł 'the Black' champions Calvinism in Lithuania and finances a Reformed church and college in Vilnius
A Catholic mob destroys the Protestant church (23 May 1591); the congregation moves out of the city
Hubmaier finds refuge under the Lords of Liechtenstein; Nikolsburg becomes an Anabaptist centre
Anabaptists form a community of goods here, origin of the Hutterites
The Synod of Debrecen adopts the Second Helvetic Confession; the town becomes the 'Calvinist Rome'
The Reformed College is founded, a leading Protestant school (Comenius taught here 1650–54)
Five Upper Hungarian royal towns adopt Leonard Stöckel's Lutheran Confessio Pentapolitana
Johannes Honterus reforms the Saxon town's church (Reformation booklet 1543)
The Lutheran confession is introduced; in 1553 the Saxon pastors elect their first Lutheran superintendent
Ferenc Dávid leads the town into Unitarianism; Prince John Sigismund follows
Péter Pázmány founds a Jesuit university; he wins much of Royal Hungary's nobility back to Catholicism
Bishop Briçonnet's reform circle offers French Scripture; later the first Calvin-inspired church in France meets here
Fourteen members of the town's Protestant church are burned
The Affair of the Placards turns Francis I against the Protestants; the capital stays Catholic
Queen Jeanne d'Albret of Navarre declares herself Calvinist and later bans Catholic worship in Béarn
Louis XIII marches into Béarn and restores Catholicism
A Protestant majority takes over the city; the Michelade (1567) kills Catholic clergy
Revocation of the Edict of Nantes: Protestant worship banned, forced conversions
Louis XIII besieges the city; the Peace of Montpellier strips its fortifications
Huguenot troops seize the city at the start of the Wars of Religion
The Edict of Amboise returns the city to royal and Catholic control
Huguenots take control of the city in April 1562
Royal troops storm Rouen in October 1562
The port becomes the Huguenots' chief stronghold
Surrenders to Richelieu after a 14-month siege; its walls are razed
Bishops and magistrates embrace Protestantism (1560); it becomes one of four Huguenot safe towns in 1570
Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (the town had submitted to the king in 1629)
Philippe Duplessis-Mornay founds the Protestant Academy of Saumur
The academy is closed (1685) and Protestant worship banned
A Calvinist regime rules the city during the Dutch Revolt
Brussels surrenders to the Duke of Parma's army; Protestants must leave
Calvinists dominate the city government of the Calvinist Republic
Fall of Antwerp to Parma; Protestants get four years to leave, many go to Amsterdam
The Calvinist Republic of Ghent is proclaimed
The Sea Beggars capture Brielle on 1 April 1572, starting the revolt in Holland
The first free assembly of the States of Holland meets here; the Synod of Dort (1618–19) fixes Reformed doctrine
Relieved from the Spanish siege; William of Orange founds a Protestant university in 1575
The Spanish garrison surrenders; Zeeland's capital turns Reformed
The 'Alteration': Catholic magistrates are expelled and the city joins the revolt
Public Catholic worship is banned in the city
The 'Reduction of Groningen' brings the city into the Dutch Republic and Reformed worship
Radical Anabaptists take over the city and proclaim a 'New Jerusalem'
The besieging prince-bishop takes the city; the leaders are executed and their bodies hung in cages
Priest Menno Simons leaves the Catholic Church and leads the peaceful Anabaptists (later Mennonites)
The Act of Supremacy makes Henry VIII head of the Church of England
Mary I restores Catholicism; about 280 Protestants are burned (1555–58)
Elizabethan Religious Settlement: the Church of England is restored; Matthew Parker becomes Archbishop of Canterbury
The Pilgrimage of Grace, a northern Catholic rising against the dissolution of the monasteries, briefly holds York
Bishop William Morgan's Welsh Bible is published
The Reformation Parliament rejects papal authority and adopts the Scots Confession
John Knox's sermon sparks iconoclastic riots in May 1559
The seat of Scotland's archbishop is reformed (Patrick Hamilton was burned here in 1528)
The Irish Parliament makes Henry VIII head of the Church of Ireland; most of the population stays Catholic
Seat of Confederate Catholic Ireland; Ireland outside the Protestant settler communities remains Catholic
The Waldensians join the Reformation at the Synod of Chanforan (small group)
Waldensian settlers in Calabria take up Reformed worship (small group)
Duchess Renée of France shelters Protestants; Calvin visits in 1536 (small group)
Renée is forced to attend Mass
A secret Protestant circle includes monks of San Isidoro del Campo (small group)
The Inquisition's autos-da-fé (1559–60) destroy the circle
Agustín de Cazalla joins a secret Protestant circle (small group)
Autos-da-fé of May and October 1559 burn the leaders
e: The Council of Constance condemns the Czech reformer Jan Hus as a heretic and burns him despite a promise of safe conduct; Bohemia rises in the Hussite revolt
Johannes Gutenberg prints the Bible with movable metal type in Mainz (first copies 1454 or 1455; about 160–185 copies, 49 survive); printing spreads the Reformation's pamphlets two generations later
Martin Luther sends his theses against the sale of indulgences to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz; whether he also nailed them to the church door is debated
Luther and Karlstadt debate Johann Eck; Luther denies that popes and councils cannot err and defends some views of Hus
Luther becomes Europe's most published author: printers distribute about 300,000 copies of his works in 1518–20. On 10 December 1520 he burns the papal bull threatening him with excommunication
Luther refuses to recant before Emperor Charles V; the Edict of Worms outlaws him and he is hidden at the Wartburg
Luther's German New Testament, translated at the Wartburg (plotted there) in about ten weeks, is printed in Wittenberg in September 1522

Peasant armies demand rights in the Twelve Articles; the princes crush them. The last major battle in Thuringia is at Frankenhausen (plotted, 14–15 May 1525); up to 100,000 of about 300,000 rebels are killed. Luther sides with the princes
Lutheran princes and cities present Melanchthon's confession of faith to Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg
The English Parliament declares Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England, breaking with Rome
Radical Anabaptists rule Münster until the prince-bishop's army takes the city in June 1535
John Calvin publishes the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion in Basel
Pope Paul III approves Ignatius of Loyola's Society of Jesus, which becomes a leading force in Catholic schools and missions
The Catholic Church's council defines doctrine against the Protestants and reforms the clergy (seminaries, residence of bishops)
Charles V defeats the Protestant Schmalkaldic League in the Schmalkaldic War
Lutheran and Catholic princes may choose their territory's faith (later summed up as 'cuius regio, eius religio'); Calvinists are excluded
Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity restore a Protestant Church of England under Elizabeth I
Image-breaking starts at Steenvoorde in Flanders on 10 August and sweeps the Low Countries, prelude to the Dutch Revolt
The Transylvanian Diet lets communities choose their preachers, a broad grant of religious freedom for its time
Catholic mobs kill Huguenots in Paris and other towns; estimates range from 5,000 to 30,000 dead
Henry IV grants the Huguenots freedom of conscience, worship in set places and safe towns, ending the French Wars of Religion
Protestant Bohemian nobles throw two imperial regents and their secretary out of a window of Prague Castle; all survive. The revolt starts the Thirty Years' War
Catholic imperial forces crush the Bohemian Protestant estates; Bohemia is re-Catholicised
Treaties of Münster and Osnabrück end the Thirty Years' War; Calvinism is recognised and 1624 becomes the 'normal year' for confessional status
Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
Louis XIV's Edict of Fontainebleau bans Protestantism in France; estimates of Protestants who left over the next two decades range from 210,000 to 900,000
